messages:
Anika: Quick question — if we move to a deny-by-default NetworkPolicy posture for private/onprem (control plane + tenant workloads), what do folks expect the perf/observability impact to be? specifically worried about: audit log ingestion rates, controller reconciliation CPU, and conntrack/eBPF pressure.
Liam: Short answer: depends on rules density and label selectors. Deny-all + many allow rules with wide selectors = more policy checks in kernel/user-space, can bump p99 packet processing and conntrack table churn.
Maya: Do we have baseline metrics? audit logs currently ~1.1k req/s at peak for small tenants, control-plane reconciliation ~150r/s. If policies cause more SYN handshake retries we could see metric blips.
Samir: We should separate concerns: 1) egress/ingress datapath cost (conntrack, iptables vs eBPF), 2) control-plane churn (k8s controller resyncs), 3) logging pipeline throughput.
Anika: Good point. I worry most about our audit pipeline (filebeat/forwarder -> kafka -> splunk). We throttle on backpressure today; want to avoid silent drops during policy rollout.
Liam: Proposal: run a small canary with tightened netpols in a staging onprem cluster with same node counts and enable conntrack + eBPF metrics. Capture: node_cpu, kube_controller_manager_reconcile_duration_seconds, node_conntrack_entries, audit_forwarder_queue_depth, and kafka_producer_retries_total.
Maya: +1. Also add packet_drop_rate and SYN retry rate from envoy ingress stats. If we see >=5% increase in retries, abort.
Samir: Here's a minimal netpol snippet to test deny-by-default for a tenant namespace — keep it narrow first then gradually widen selectors:
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-tenant-a
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress: []
  egress: []
```
Start with that, then add explicit allow rules for kube-dns, kube-apiserver, prometheus metrics scraper.
Anika: For audit log safety, let's flip audit-forwarder to buffered mode with backpressure alerting: set buffer.max_bytes=50MB and alerts if queue > 10k entries. Samir can you draft the forwarder config?
Samir: Will do. Example forwarding flag: `--buffered=true --max-queue-size=10000` and add a CloudWatch/Sentry alert for queue depth.
Liam: One more: quantify cost of eBPF vs iptables using sysbench-like microbench. Use tcpreplay to create a mix of 70% small payloads (LLM request style) and 30% large payloads (embeddings) to mimic real load.
Maya: I'll own the benchmark harness (k6 + tcpreplay) and collect the metrics. Can we also snapshot kube-apiserver audit logs sizes? that affects disk IO and forwarder CPU.
Anika: Owner summary: Maya -> run benchmarks and collect metrics; Liam -> provide eBPF vs iptables test plan and node image; Samir -> update forwarder buffered config + alerts; Anika -> coordinate canary window and rollback playbook.
deploy-bot: test-run STARTED for canary netpol-tightening on staging-onprem-2 (run id: cr-2026-03-21-01). Logs: https://ci.internal/reports/cr-2026-03-21-01
Maya: Kicking off run now. ETA 90m for full sweep, will post a short dashboard link when metrics are in.
Anika: Thanks team. If we see audit pipeline >20% CPU increase or queue growth >5k within first 30m, auto-rollback. tagging @oncall and @infra for visibility. :eyes:
Liam: Also note: RBAC won't need changes unless we create forwarding sidecars that require new ServiceAccount scopes. If so, we'll do least-privileged svcacc and scoped KMS decrypt permission for forwarder keys.
Samir: For KMS, prefer using KMS envelope keys on node HSM if available. If not, use customer KMS with short-lived node tokens and rotate every hour.
Maya: Will include KMS latency in bench (avg and p95). that can affect forwarder latency.
Anika: Great. We'll reconvene after results. If benchmarks are clean, we'll draft a gradual rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automated rollback triggers.
Liam: 👍
Maya: :rocket:
Samir: Filed follow-up runbook here: https://wiki.internal/security/netpol-tightening-runbook (WIP)
